personality_voice.book_baseline: In the book corpus, Voldemort's personality is conveyed mostly through reports, legend, and his brief direct appearance at the end of Philosopher's Stone. He is imperious, contemptuous of weakness, ruthless toward followers and enemies alike, and ideologically coherent: power is the only truth, and those who do not seek it are fools. His direct speech is cold, seductive, and threateningly paternalistic — he flatters Harry's bravery while simultaneously threatening him, offers him his parents as bait, and frames everything as rational inevitability. Key lines: 'Don't be a fool... Better save your own life and join me'; 'I always value bravery... your parents were brave'; 'They died begging me for mercy.' He also shows a capacity for theatrical cruelty — correcting Harry's perception of events ('Your mother needn't have died') to destabilize him emotionally. Through Quirrell's account, he is established as demanding, punitive toward failure ('He does not forgive mistakes easily'), and ideologically persuasive ('There is no good and evil, there is only power'). His voice even when disembodied is described as 'high' — a detail reinforcing his inhuman register.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film preserves the core ideological lines almost verbatim: 'There is no good and evil, there is only power, and those too weak to seek it' is retained. His offer to reunite Harry with his parents is present, as is his commanding tone toward Quirrell ('Stop him!', 'Kill him!', 'Fool, get the Stone!'). He addresses Harry directly and by name. His disembodied face on the back of Quirrell's head is depicted as chalk-white and snake-like. The seductive-threatening duality is preserved in the film exchange: he frames joining him as the rational choice, then pivots immediately to lethal command when refused.
personality_voice.difference: The film compresses Voldemort's speech significantly. The book version delivers a longer, more nuanced manipulation — acknowledging Harry's bravery, describing the deaths of his parents with deliberately calibrated cruelty ('your father put up a courageous fight'), and exploiting Harry's emotional vulnerability over multiple beats. The film collapses this into a shorter exchange and replaces the parents-dying detail with an offer to bring them back (a manipulation, but a different one — more sentimental bait than cold cruelty). The book's 'They died begging me for mercy' — a direct, vicious lie designed to wound — is absent from the film. The film Voldemort is slightly more transactional and less psychologically sadistic in this scene. Additionally, the book's 'He lies... He lies...' disembodied interjection during Quirrell's interrogation is absent from the film corpus, removing one instance of Voldemort asserting control from an invisible position.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The main personality traits — imperious, ideologically coherent, contemptuous of weakness, manipulative toward Harry — are preserved. The compression removes the sharpest edge of his psychological cruelty (the parents-begging line) and reduces the theatrical multi-beat manipulation to a shorter arc. This is a minor but real simplification of his voice — the book Voldemort is more precisely calibrated in his cruelty; the film version is recognizable but slightly flatter. Score reflects preservation of core traits with minor loss of the most cutting behavioral texture.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In the book, Voldemort functions across the entire first book as the absent, structuring threat — the reason Harry is famous, the reason the wizarding world is fearful, the reason Quirrell is compromised, and the reason the Stone must be protected. He is the ultimate cause of the main plot. In the climactic scene, he is a genuine antagonist with agency: he speaks independently, directs Quirrell's actions in real time ('Seize him!', 'Kill him, fool, and be done!', 'KILL HIM! KILL HIM!'), attempts to bargain with Harry, and when bargaining fails, orders lethal escalation. He also functions as the source of ideological corruption — Quirrell's account establishes that Voldemort persuaded a naive young man to abandon belief in good and evil, demonstrating active philosophical seduction as a power. Dumbledore's post-climax explanation further assigns him a structural role: he left Quirrell to die, showing that his abandonment of followers is a defining trait that has narrative consequence.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The film preserves Voldemort's role as the structuring absent threat and his real-time command of Quirrell in the climax. He speaks, he directs, he attempts to seduce Harry, he commands killing. His role as the reason for Harry's fame is preserved through Hagrid's narration and the Ollivander scene. His abandonment of Quirrell is implied structurally (Quirrell crumbles, Voldemort's spirit flies free) even if not explicitly stated.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The book's 'He left Quirrell to die; he shows just as little mercy to his followers as his enemies' (Dumbledore's explanation) is absent from the film's hospital wing scene. The film's Dumbledore does not articulate this. This removes one explicit confirmation of a defining behavioral pattern — that Voldemort treats followers as expendable. Additionally, Quirrell's detailed account of Voldemort punishing him for the Gringotts failure is present in the book but absent in the film; the film Quirrell does not describe Voldemort's punitive behavior toward him at all, reducing the texture of Voldemort's relationship with his servants. The book's disembodied 'He lies... He lies...' moment (Voldemort asserting control by contradicting Quirrell mid-interrogation) is absent from the film, removing one instance of Voldemort exercising agency while invisible.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Voldemort's primary narrative function — structuring threat, climactic antagonist, ideological corrupting force — is preserved. The losses are in secondary confirmatory moments that reinforce specific behavioral traits (cruelty to followers, disembodied control). These are real but not primary agency losses. The score reflects a role and agency that is recognizably preserved with some compression of the behavioral evidence that supports that role.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Voldemort's motivations in the book corpus are: (1) return to bodily existence and full power, (2) acquisition of the Philosopher's Stone as the instrument of that return, (3) elimination of Harry Potter, who represents both a past failure and a potential future threat. His motivation is not portrayed as internally conflicted — he is single-minded and ideologically unified. However, the book does establish a specific motivational texture: he endures a degraded, parasitic existence because he will not accept death, and he is willing to inhabit another's body and sustain himself on unicorn blood as temporary measures. This is not internal conflict but rather a coherent hierarchy of survival over dignity. The ideological underpinning — 'there is no good and evil, there is only power' — is presented as his sincere worldview, not rationalisation.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film preserves all three primary motivations. The parasitic existence is foregrounded in Voldemort's direct speech to Harry: 'You see what I've become? See what I must do to survive? Live off another. A mere parasite.' The Stone as instrument of return is explicit. The targeting of Harry is explicit. The ideology ('there is no good and evil, there is only power') is retained verbatim. The offer of Harry's parents as bait adds a sentimental manipulation absent from the book scene, but this is consistent with his established pattern of exploiting vulnerability to seek compliance.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The film actually adds the parents-as-bait offer, which the book does not include in the mirror scene (the book uses the parents' deaths as a weapon of cruelty, not as a promised reward). This is a mild invention — not incoherent with his character, but a slightly different motivational surface. The book's deeper texture of Voldemort's willingness to punish followers who fail him (establishing that his survival drive overrides even loyalty) is less developed in the film. Quirrell's account of being punished for the Gringotts failure, which supports this, is absent.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Core motivations are intact and explicitly stated in the film. The parents-bait addition is a minor invention that does not contradict the book characterization. The absence of the punishment-of-followers thread slightly thins the motivational texture but does not alter or replace any core motivation. Score reflects motivations that are simplified in texture but substantially correct.

character_arc.book_baseline: Within the scope of Philosopher's Stone, Voldemort has no arc in the traditional sense — he is in a state of degraded limbo at the start and remains in that state at the end, having failed to acquire the Stone. His 'arc' in this book is purely functional: he attempts restoration, is foiled, and retreats. This is an intentionally flat arc for this installment; his larger arc across the series (from absence to partial return to full return to defeat) begins here but is not concluded. The corpus establishes his starting position: disembodied, parasitic, not truly alive and therefore unable to be truly killed.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film mirrors this exactly. Voldemort begins the story as a disembodied threat, appears embodied only through Quirrell, fails to acquire the Stone, and retreats as a spirit. Dumbledore's explanation in the film — 'I'm afraid there are ways in which he can return' — parallels the book's acknowledgment that he remains a persistent threat.
character_arc.difference: The book's Dumbledore explicitly states 'He is still out there somewhere, perhaps looking for another body to share... not being truly alive, he cannot be killed. He left Quirrell to die.' The film's Dumbledore omits the 'left Quirrell to die' observation and is slightly less specific about the nature of Voldemort's continued existence, but retains the essential point that he can return. The arc's functional beats — failed attempt, retreat, persistent threat — are all present.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc within this book is flat and intentionally so; the film matches this. The minor compression of Dumbledore's explanation does not alter the arc's trajectory or meaning. The score is near the top of the compressed-but-faithful range, with a small deduction for the omission of the Quirrell-abandonment observation which is part of the arc's closing beat.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Two key relationships are established in the corpus. (1) Voldemort and Quirrell: the book establishes a master-servant dynamic defined by Voldemort's absolute authority, Quirrell's fearful submission, and Voldemort's punitive cruelty toward failure. Quirrell explicitly describes being punished, describes finding it hard to follow instructions, describes Voldemort as demanding. This is a relationship of total domination with the servant living in physical and psychological terror. (2) Voldemort and Harry: established as a defining antagonism — the man who killed his parents, who failed to kill Harry, and who now represents Harry's central fear and destiny. In the climactic scene, Voldemort attempts to manipulate Harry using his parents, threatens him, and commands his death — a relationship of power, hatred, and a strange acknowledgment ('I always value bravery').
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Voldemort-Quirrell dynamic is preserved in broad strokes: Voldemort commands, Quirrell obeys, Quirrell shows fear ('Master, you are not strong enough'). The Voldemort-Harry antagonism is preserved: Harry recognizes Voldemort, Voldemort addresses him by name, attempts manipulation, commands his death. The film adds the parents-in-the-mirror bait, which intensifies the exploitation dynamic.
key_relationships.difference: The film removes Quirrell's extended account of being punished by Voldemort for the Gringotts failure, which is the primary evidence in the book for the texture of the Voldemort-Quirrell relationship (not just command-obedience, but active punishment of failure, fear as the operational mode of service). Without this, the film's Quirrell-Voldemort relationship reads as domination without the specific punitive cruelty that defines it in the book. The 'he does not forgive mistakes easily' dimension is absent. The Voldemort-Harry relationship loses the specific cruelty of 'They died begging me for mercy' — a line that defines Voldemort's willingness to exploit grief as a weapon — and replaces it with the parents-as-bait offer, which is a different (if related) manipulative mode.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Both key relationships are recognizable and functionally preserved. The Quirrell relationship loses its most defining textural element (punitive cruelty, Quirrell's fear-of-failure). The Harry relationship loses its sharpest emotional weapon (the begging line) but gains a different manipulation. These are real alterations to the emotional dynamics of both relationships — not merely compression but replacement and reduction in specific texture. The score reflects relationships that are mostly faithful in function but altered in the specific dynamics that make them distinctive.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Within this single book's corpus, Voldemort's complexity is limited but specific. He is not merely a monster — he is ideologically coherent, strategically patient (willing to survive in degraded form rather than risk permanent death), psychologically sophisticated in manipulation (calibrating cruelty to wound Harry emotionally about his parents), and capable of a strange form of acknowledgment ('I always value bravery'). He treats his servant as both tool and burden, showing that his relationships are entirely transactional. The book also establishes, through Dumbledore, that the one thing Voldemort cannot understand is love — framing his complexity through a specific incapacity rather than a simple evil-label. Quirrell's account ('A foolish young man I was then... Lord Voldemort showed me how wrong I was') establishes Voldemort as an active ideological seducer, not merely a violent tyrant.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film preserves the ideological coherence and the love-incapacity (Dumbledore's explanation is retained). The seductive manipulation is present in the climax. The transactional treatment of Quirrell is structurally present.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The film removes: (1) Quirrell's detailed description of being persuaded and then punished — the account of Voldemort as an ideological seducer who then becomes punitive is largely absent; (2) the 'They died begging me for mercy' line, which is the most specific evidence of Voldemort's psychological sadism and his willingness to construct false narratives to wound; (3) the 'He lies... He lies...' disembodied interjection; (4) Dumbledore's 'He left Quirrell to die; he shows just as little mercy to his followers as his enemies' — which is the most explicit statement of Voldemort's complete transactionality. These losses collectively reduce the nuance: the film Voldemort is recognizable as a ruthless power-seeker, but the specific textures of his psychological sadism, ideological seduction capacity, and follower-abandonment pattern are thinner.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The character remains recognizable and the primary complexity markers (ideological coherence, love-incapacity, manipulative intelligence) are present. However, multiple specific nuances — the punitive cruelty toward Quirrell, the sadistic parental-begging lie, the follower-abandonment as explicit character statement — are absent without replacement. This is noticeable simplification of the book's characterization of Voldemort's specific texture. Score reflects a character who is substantially present but with important nuances missing.

lost_or_transferred_material: 'They died begging me for mercy' — Voldemort's lie designed to wound Harry emotionally, present in the book climax, absent from the film

Quirrell's account of Voldemort punishing him for the Gringotts failure ('He does not forgive mistakes easily... He punished me') — establishes the punitive texture of the master-servant dynamic, absent from the film
'He lies... He lies...' — Voldemort's disembodied interjection asserting control during Quirrell's interrogation of Harry, absent from the film

Dumbledore's statement 'He left Quirrell to die; he shows just as little mercy to his followers as his enemies' — explicit confirmation of a defining behavioral pattern, absent from the film's hospital wing scene

Voldemort's multi-beat psychological manipulation of Harry in the climax (acknowledging bravery, then describing the father's courageous fight, then offering the mother's life as a bargaining chip) — compressed and partially replaced in the film with the parents-in-the-mirror offer

score_caps_applied: Cap 3 (score not above 75 if core book functions, decisions, or emotional beats are transferred or removed): The 'They died begging me for mercy' line and Quirrell's punishment account are absent without transfer to another character, constituting removal rather than transfer. However, the losses are not full transfers to another character but rather omissions. Cap 3 is assessed as borderline applicable given the partial nature of the loss; the score of 71 already falls below 75 and reflects this.

Cap 1 (score not above 85 if films remove a major part of complexity, agency, contradiction, or narrative function): Applied — multiple specific nuances are absent; the score of 71 respects this ceiling.
key_observations: The film's portrayal of Voldemort in Philosopher's Stone is recognizable and preserves the primary characterization: ideological coherence, ruthless domination of Quirrell, manipulative antagonism toward Harry, parasitic existence, and the love-incapacity that Dumbledore identifies. The ideology ('there is no good and evil, there is only power') is retained verbatim, and the climactic dynamic is structurally faithful. However, several specific nuances that define Voldemort's particular texture in the book are absent: his psychological sadism in the parental-begging lie, the punitive cruelty toward Quirrell that makes the master-servant dynamic more than mere command-obedience, and Dumbledore's explicit statement that he abandoned Quirrell to die. The film adds the parents-in-the-mirror manipulation, which is not incoherent but represents a different (softer, more sentimental) form of exploitation than the book's colder cruelty. The cumulative effect is a Voldemort who is broadly faithful but somewhat stripped of the specific behavioral edges that make him psychologically precise. The confidence is Medium throughout because the corpus covers only one book and its film adaptation, limiting the comparative depth available.
